newsitem.title: USA: U.N. chief meets U.S. leaders seeking dues payment.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief meets U.S. leaders seeking dues payment.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan met U.S. political leaders on Thursday as he embarked on an uphill battle to get Washington to pay its huge debt that is crippling the United Nations.
Annan called on Under Secretary of State Peter Tarnoff and was scheduled to meet President Bill Clinton later in the day.

In speaking to administration officials, Annan is essentially preaching to the converted -- they agree the United States should pay its debts. The real struggle is with members of Congress who have blocked past payment of dues.

Annan was also due to meet on Thursday with a foe of the United Nations, Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms. His schedule also included House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich and Senate majority leader Trent Lott, both Republicans.

Republican leaders have expressed willingness to pay off the more than $1 billion the United States owes the United Nations but have attached conditions that appear beyond the power of any U.N. chief to deliver.

New York Republican Benjamin Gilman, chairman of the House International Relations Committee, told Annan Wednesday U.S. dues should be lowered from 25 percent to 20 percent of the U.N. regular budget, which is calculated by members' wealth.
According to those at the meeting, Gilman also said U.N. salaries could not be raised and the world body would have to issue a "code of conduct" which he did not spell out.

While legally the United States owes the United Nations $1.3 billion, the calculation in Washington is $500 million less because of unilateral deductions by Congress over the years, especially since Republicans came to power in 1994.

But Annan, speaking to reporters after an early morning meeting with Cesar Gaviria, secretary general of the Organisation of American States, declared himself "very hopeful" about the outcome of his Washington trip.

"I think I had a very good start yesterday and if I have another good day today and tomorrow I think I can go back to New York with, I would not say assurances, but high optimism that it won't be long before the right decisions are taken and the checks follow," he said.
"What is important is that we do not focus only on the arrears but commitments to future assessments," he added.
Annan pledged that reform of the U.N. bureaucracy -- a key demand of the organisation's U.S. critics -- was going ahead.
"But we need all member states on board and we can't do it on a shoestring budget. So the payments must be made and on my part I undertake to pursue vigorously the reform of the U.N.," he said.

Annan, who met Wednesday with Vice-President Al Gore, said administration officials were "all very supportive" and he sensed a "new beginning" in relations with Washington. He said it was symbolic that he was Clinton's first prominent visitor since the president's second-term inauguration Monday.

At her swearing-in ceremony, incoming Secretary of State Madeleine Albright noted her first official act would be attending the Annan-Clinton meeting and said that was "a very god sign of the support that the United States is going to give to the United Nations."
Annan, a 58-year old Ghanaian, took office in January with the backing of the Clinton administration. His reform plans have to be approved by U.N. members.
Unlike his predecessor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt, he intends to draw up a blueprint by mid-year rather than leave it to the 185 member states to take the initiative.
